title: If the world hates you (John 15:18–27)
hook: a warning that following him won't always be popular

segments.voice: Yesterday, greater love, and a new name: I have called you friends. Your line was not servants, friends. Did you do the favor? Day six hundred thirty-six.

Most recruiting pitches lead with the good news. Join us: great team, real purpose, benefits from day one. The hard parts come later, in the fine print, if at all. Jesus has just told his friends they are chosen, loved, let in on the plan. And then, in the very same breath, he does something no recruiter would do. He tells them the hard part. Plainly, at the table, with no fine print. People will not always like you for this. Some will hate you. Today, the warning.
screen: `RECRUITERS SAVE THE HARD PART FOR LATER.`

segments.voice: In the King James Bible: "If the world hate you, ye know that it hated me before it hated you." The world here is the Greek word kosmos. And John uses it in a surprising double way. In chapter three, God so loved the world. Here, the world hates. Same word. Here the world seems to mean not the planet or nature or ordinary life, but people and powers organized as if God weren't there. In John's telling, God loves it, and it often doesn't love back. So the warning isn't that the disciples should hate the world. It's that they shouldn't be shocked when the world pushes against them. Then Jesus reminds them of something he said at the foot washing: "The servant is not greater than his lord." If they treated me this way, he says, don't expect better. And he quotes a line of scripture, one readers find in the Psalms: "They hated me without a cause." There's a comfort folded inside the warning, and it's in that small word before. It hated me before it hated you. The disciples won't be the first; he has gone through it ahead of them. The passage ends with a promise and a job. The Comforter, the Spirit of truth, will testify, and so will they, "because ye have been with me from the beginning." Christians have read these verses in very different times. Where believers have faced real persecution, in the early centuries and in places today, the words have been a lifeline. In comfortable places, some readers take them as a warning against two things: seeking approval at any cost, and mistaking ordinary criticism for persecution.
screen: `THE SERVANT IS NOT GREATER THAN HIS LORD.`
`IT HATED ME FIRST: HE WENT AHEAD.`
`THE SPIRIT TESTIFIES, AND SO WILL YOU.`
then, large: `IT HATED ME BEFORE IT HATED YOU.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: stay kind when disliked. Settle, and breathe. Think of someone who doesn't like you. A coworker, an in-law, a neighbor, someone online. Notice what happens in your body when you picture them. The tight jaw, the speech you're already rehearsing. Breathe into that. Now picture one small kindness you could show them anyway. Not to win them over. Just because kindness doesn't need their approval. If you pray, you can pray for them by name. If you don't, simply wish them well. The bell holds the time.
Kosmos. The Greek word behind the world, used two ways in John: the world God loves, and the world that hates him.
Your line: it hated me first. Today, when someone is cold to you, answer with one small kindness, and let it stand without needing a reply. Day six hundred thirty-six.

howItsDone: Christians in places where faith brings danger often read John 15 as words of courage, and some churches set aside a day each year to pray for Christians who are persecuted.

original.note: Greek: order, adornment, the world. in John it can mean the world God loves (3:16) and the world that hates him (15:18).

trapdoor: what you thought: a warning that everybody will hate Christians.
what it means: don't be shocked if following him isn't popular; he went through it first, and you're not alone.
what a scholar hears: kosmos in John is double-edged, loved in 3:16 and hostile in 15:18, and 'without a cause' echoes Psalms 35:19 and 69:4.
recall: thou hast the words of eternal life

notes: Definition of kosmos in John as 'people and powers organized as if God weren't there' is an interpretive summary common in commentaries. Confirm.
John 15:25 cites 'their law'; the source is usually identified as Psalm 35:19 or 69:4. Confirm.
The closing contrast between persecuted and comfortable settings is descriptive; the line about mistaking criticism for persecution should be checked for tone.
howItsDone: several churches keep an annual day of prayer for the persecuted church (dates differ). Confirm phrasing.

Editor review (y2 pass): 15:25 says 'written in their law', so the script no longer has Jesus 'quote the Psalms' (readers trace it there); the kosmos definition and 'God loves it' are now framed as John's usage, not narrator fact; cut the stock 'you're not alone' (voice and screen head); 'Christians often' and 'many churches' softened.
